title: The Rabbit Nation and the Elephant
intro: An elephant takes to walking through the rabbits’ home. Shawqi brings their scholars, poets and writers to a meeting where three elected speakers propose three ways out of danger. When the rabbits offer a crown to the one whose plan saved them, he remembers who first called them together.

translation: The story goes that the rabbit nation
had taken a corner of the earth for its own.
1.sharh: The storyteller’s “they say” introduces a people already dignified with the name of nation. Its territory takes up only a corner of the earth.

translation: They rejoiced in their good country,
a shelter for their families and womenfolk.
2.sharh: Home means somewhere dependants can be kept safe. The rabbits have something concrete to defend before the story gives them an enemy.

translation: The elephant chose it for his road
and tore our friends to pieces.
3.sharh: For the elephant this is a choice of route. For those in its path it means dismemberment. “Our friends” quietly places the teller among the rabbits.

translation: Among them lived a rabbit of good sense.
Experience had worn most of his fleece away.
4.sharh: The familiar joke about a veteran going bald is made in rabbit terms. Experience has taken its toll in fur and furnished him with something to say.

translation: “Company of rabbits,” he called to them,
“scholar, poet and writer alike,
5.sharh: The old rabbit summons people by their occupations. A community of apparently interchangeable animals turns out to contain different kinds of intelligence.

translation: unite against this brutal enemy.
Union is the strength of the weak.”
6.sharh: The old rabbit’s first proposal concerns the way a decision can be made. He gives the community a source of strength it can use before it has settled on a plan.

translation: They came, finding his judgement sound,
and raised a banner for the meeting.
7.sharh: His opinion, ra’y, gives rise to a banner, raya. The echo helps turn a private judgement into something everyone can gather round.

translation: They chose three from among themselves,
giving weight to neither age nor youth.
8.sharh: The assembly elects speakers of its own. Respect for the old rabbit who called it together has not made seniority an electoral rule.

translation: They looked for ripeness of mind
and counted worth in years of its own.
9.sharh: The language of age survives the rejection of an age test. Good judgement has a maturity of its own, which need not coincide with the body’s.

translation: The first rose to address them.
“The sound course,” he said,
10.sharh: The first man to take the floor labels his proposal sound in advance. The little delay across the line leaves the audience waiting to hear what it actually costs.

translation: “is to leave the land to the lord of the trunk
and have peace from the tyrant’s harm.”
11.sharh: The elephant figures as the owner of a magnificent trunk. The speaker would allow him to become the owner of the rabbits’ land as well.

translation: Our dear rabbits raised a cry.
“That would hurt us more than the father of terrors.”
12.sharh: The elephant’s grand nickname belongs to the previous speaker’s adversary. The assembly reserves its sharpest criticism for the proposal meant to save it.

translation: The second sprang up. “In the fox
I know an old master of the art.
13.sharh: The next speaker sees professional expertise for hire. An audience of rabbits has good reason to consider what a fox’s professional expertise usually consists of.

translation: Let us call him in to lend us his wisdom
and take two rabbits as his fee.”
14.sharh: “Two” stands quite naked in the Arabic. The speaker has reduced two members of the assembly to a fee payable to their natural predator.

translation: “No, Your Highness,” came the answer.
“An enemy cannot ward off an enemy.”
15.sharh: A ceremonious form of address softens the blunt refusal. The fee has already shown what sort of ally the assembly would be admitting.

translation: The third volunteered to speak.
“My fellow peoples,” he said,
16.sharh: The third speaker’s opening recalls the summons that made the meeting possible. His proposal will grow directly out of the old rabbit’s idea.

translation: “Gather together, for gathering is strength.
Then dig a hollow in the road.
17.sharh: The speaker repeats the call for union and gives the assembled rabbits a job it takes a community to do. The road itself becomes their means of deliverance.

translation: The elephant will tumble in as he passes.
We shall have peace from him for good.
18.sharh: The phrase about having peace echoes the first proposal. This time the rabbits can imagine that peace in their own home.

translation: Generation after generation will tell
how the rabbit ate the elephant’s wits.”
19.sharh: To “eat his wits” is to outwit him utterly. The figure lends the little vegetarian a memorable appetite for one line.

translation: They approved his words and liked them well,
then went straight to work and did it well.
20.sharh: Two Arabic verbs built on goodness mark successive acts, finding the suggestion good and doing the work well. The rabbits make the move between them at once.

translation: The elephant of high estate perished.
The nation spent the evening safe.
21.sharh: The elephant’s high estate carries a hint of physical height after his fall. The rabbits can at last spend an ordinary evening in safety.

translation: They came hurrying to the author of the plan,
bringing the crown and throne.
22.sharh: The originator of the successful plan finds himself offered two tangible things, a crown and a seat. The story could end in a coronation here.

translation: “Gently, children of these lands.
My rightful place is second.
23.sharh: The third speaker claims second place with some precision. He knows what his idea was worth and can name the contribution on which it depended.

translation: The voice that rang out strong and carried the day
was the one that called, ‘Company of rabbits.’”
24.sharh: The quoted words take us back to the fifth couplet. The rabbit gives first place to the voice that made it possible for anyone, himself included, to be heard.

1.1.3.head: أُمَّة
1.1.3.meaning: A people or nation, the name given to the rabbits before any threat arrives.

1.2.4.meaning: Soil or earth, the actual ground of the rabbits’ country.

2.2.1.head: مَوئِل
2.2.1.meaning: A refuge, a place to which one can return for safety.

2.2.2-3.head: العِيال وَالحَريم
2.2.2-3.meaning: Dependants and the women of the household, a traditional description of those a home shelters.

3.1.4.head: طَريق
3.1.4.meaning: A route or right of passage, the elephant’s use for land already inhabited as a home.

3.2.2.head: أَصحاب
3.2.2.meaning: “Our friends”, an affectionate narrator’s aside that draws the audience into the story.

4.2.2.head: جُلّ
4.2.2.meaning: The greater part or bulk of something.

4.2.4.head: التَّجريب
4.2.4.meaning: Experience earned by living through things. Shawqi pictures its cost as wear on a coat of fur.

5.1.4.head: مَعشَر
5.1.4.meaning: A company addressed together on the strength of something its members share.

6.1.4.meaning: Harsh or brutal in dealing with others.

7.1.2.head: مُستَصوِب
7.1.2.meaning: Finding an opinion sound and giving it one’s approval.

7.1.3.head: رَأي
7.1.3.meaning: Counsel or judgement. Ra’y leads by sound into raya, the banner raised in response.

7.2.1-3.head: عَقَدَ رايَة
7.2.1-3.meaning: “Tied a banner”, raised a standard as a visible point of assembly.

8.2.3.head: راعى
8.2.3.meaning: Took into account when weighing candidates.

9.2.4-5.head: سِنّ الفَضل
9.2.4-5.meaning: “The age of merit”, a maturity measured in worth and judgement.

10.2.4-5.head: ذو الصَّواب
10.2.4-5.meaning: “Possessed of soundness”, the course that the first speaker is about to commend.

11.1.4-5.head: ذو الخُرطوم
11.1.4-5.meaning: “The one with the trunk”, the elephant identified by his most conspicuous feature.

11.2.5.head: الغَشوم
11.2.5.meaning: An oppressive brute who harms indiscriminately.

12.1.3.meaning: Dear or precious, the narrator’s affectionate name for his rabbits.

12.2.4-5.head: أَبو الأَهوال
12.2.4-5.meaning: “Father of terrors”, the elephant’s nickname here. Abu al-Hawl is also a name for the Sphinx.

13.2.1.head: عَهِدَ
13.2.1.meaning: Knew from experience. The second rabbit offers the fox’s reputation as grounds for hiring him.

13.2.4-5.head: شَيخ الفَنّ
13.2.4-5.meaning: “Master of the art”, the fox’s long-standing reputation for cunning.

14.1.1.head: دَعا
14.1.1.meaning: Summoned someone to attend. The object pronoun refers to the fox.

14.2.2.head: اِثنان
14.2.2.meaning: Two of the rabbits themselves. The speaker leaves the commodity unnamed.

15.1.4-5.head: صاحِب السُّمُوّ
15.1.4-5.meaning: “Your Highness”, a princely form of address used in the assembly’s retort.

16.1.1.head: اِنتَدَبَ
16.1.1.meaning: Volunteered or rose of one’s own accord.

18.2.2.head: الدَّهر
18.2.2.meaning: For all time, throughout the future the speaker imagines for the nation.

19.2.2-5.head: أَكَلَ عَقلَهُ
19.2.2-5.meaning: “Ate his wits”, got the better of him by cunning.

20.1.2.head: مَقال
20.1.2.meaning: An address or proposal, here the third rabbit’s plan for digging the pit.

20.2.2-3.meaning: Straight away, while the impulse to act is still fresh.

21.1.4.head: الشّان
21.1.4.meaning: Standing or estate. The normally audible glottal stop in sha’n is eased in the rhyme.

21.2.1.head: أَمسى
21.2.1.meaning: Reached evening in a given state, also “became”. The rabbits can spend the evening safely on their own ground.

22.1.2-3.head: صاحِب التَّدبير
22.1.2-3.meaning: “The author of the plan”, the third speaker who proposed digging the pit.

22.2.3.head: السَّرير
22.2.3.meaning: A royal throne, brought with the crown.

23.1.3-4.head: بَنو الأَوطان
23.1.3-4.meaning: “Children of the homelands”, a civic address to the animals whose home was threatened.

23.2.2.head: مَحَلّ
23.2.2.meaning: Place or rank in the order of credit.

24.2.4-6.head: يا مَعشَرَ الأَرانِب
24.2.4-6.meaning: “Company of rabbits”, the opening call in couplet 5. Quoting it identifies the elder to whom the speaker gives first place.
